amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-01.title: Fold each shape
amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-01.body:
A shape has a line of symmetry if you can fold it along a line so that the two halves match exactly.

* **(A)** The triangle has two equal sides. A line straight down through the top corner and the middle of the bottom side folds it onto itself. ✓
* **(B)** The step shape matches itself when turned half-way round, but no fold makes the halves match.
* **(C)** The right-angled triangle has three different side lengths, so no fold works.
* **(D)** The straight arm on one side and the round part on the other never match.
* **(E)** The three arms all bend the same way (like a pinwheel), so a mirror image would bend the other way.

**Answer: (A)**

amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-01.title: Look at the mirror images
amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-01.body:
Imagine each shape in a mirror. A shape has a line of symmetry exactly when its mirror image can be placed directly on top of the original.

For (B), (C), (D) and (E) the mirror image faces the "wrong way" and cannot be laid over the original, however you slide or turn it. Only the triangle in (A), with its two equal sloping sides, matches its mirror image.

**Answer: (A)**

amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-02.title: Work out Naida's age first
amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-02.body:
* Cecily is 10 years older than Naida, so Naida is $42-10=32$.
* Naida is 6 years younger than Joycelyn, so Joycelyn is $32+6=38$.

**Answer: (D) 38**

amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-02.title: Compare Cecily and Joycelyn directly
amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-02.body:
Cecily is 10 years older than Naida, and Joycelyn is only 6 years older than Naida. So Cecily is $10-6=4$ years older than Joycelyn, and Joycelyn is $42-4=38$.

**Answer: (D) 38**

amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-03.title: Try the big L along the edges
amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-03.body:
The square has $16$ small squares. The two shapes shown use $5$ (the 'S') and $6$ (the 'L'), so the third shape uses $16-11=5$ squares.

The long 'L' is the hardest to place, so put it in first. It has to lie along the edges of the square: either with both arms along two sides, or with only its short arm along a side.

Now try to fit the 'S'. It only fits when both arms of the L are along the sides, and there is only one place for it that leaves the remaining empty squares in **one** piece:
$$\begin{array}{cccc} S&S&\square&\square\\ L&S&\square&\square\\ L&S&S&\square\\ L&L&L&L \end{array}$$
The empty squares $\square$ form a $2\times2$ block with one more square underneath — exactly shape (B).

**Answer: (B)**

amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-04.title: Count winning and losing rolls
amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-04.body:
A dice has $6$ equally likely numbers, so a game is fair when exactly $3$ numbers win and $3$ lose.

| Game | Winning rolls | Losing rolls |
|---|---|---|
| (A) | 6 | 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 |
| (B) | 2, 5 | 1, 3, 4, 6 |
| (C) | 5, 6 | 1, 2, 3, 4 |
| (D) | 1, 2 | 3, 4, 5, 6 |
| (E) | 1, 3, 5 | 2, 4, 6 |

Only game (E) has $3$ winning and $3$ losing rolls.

**Answer: (E)**

amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-04.title: Odd and even
amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-04.body:
Half of the numbers $1$–$6$ are odd ($1,3,5$) and half are even ($2,4,6$). So "win on an odd number" gives the same chance of winning as of losing. The other games each win on only $1$ or $2$ of the $6$ numbers, so you lose more often than you win.

**Answer: (E)**

amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-05.title: Find the magic sum
amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-05.body:
The nine numbers add up to $2+4+6+8+10+12+14+16+18=90$. The three rows share this total equally, so each row (and each column and diagonal) adds up to $90\div3=30$.

* Right column: top shaded square $= 30-6-16 = 8$.
* Middle row: centre shaded square $= 30-14-6=10$.

The shaded squares add up to $8+10=18$.

**Answer: (C) 18**

amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-05.title: Use the centre
amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-05.body:
In a $3\times3$ magic square made of equally spaced numbers, the middle number of the list goes in the centre. The list $2,4,\dots,18$ has middle number $10$, so the centre is $10$, and each line adds to $3\times10=30$.

The top-right square is then $30-6-16=8$, and $8+10=18$.

**Answer: (C) 18**

amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-06.title: Count by first digit
amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-06.body:
* From $100$ to $199$, a palindrome must start and end with $1$: $101, 111, 121, \ldots, 191$. The middle digit can be $0$–$9$, so there are $10$.
* From $200$ to $299$, similarly $202, 212, \ldots, 292$: another $10$.
* $300$ is not a palindrome ($003$ backwards).

Total: $10+10=20$.

**Answer: 20**

amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-06.title: Choose the digits
amt-amc-practice-1-mpr-06.body:
A three-digit palindrome looks like $\overline{aba}$. To be between $100$ and $300$, the first digit $a$ must be $1$ or $2$ ($2$ choices), and the middle digit $b$ can be any of $0$–$9$ ($10$ choices). That gives $2\times10=20$ palindromes.

**Answer: 20**
